pages.description: When learners commit an individual answer to a conceptual question and then discuss their reasoning with peers, later independent answers to a new isomorphic question may improve, conditional on the question, group dynamics, instructor follow-up and an immediate horizon.
pages.title: Peer Discussion

pages.description: For learners who have already studied the material, a structured exchange in which each must explain to a peer and answer that peer's questions (tutoring, teaching a peer, reciprocal roles, peer assessment) is expected to raise each learner's individually measured achievement over studying alone, for explainer and helped alike; meta-analyses test peer tutoring against no tutoring and teaching against studying, while no claim tests the doses, role rotation or hand-over points.
pages.title: Peer Learning

pages.description: Where learners sharing one goal differ in prior knowledge, interests, access needs or preferred means, tailoring support, pace, problem contexts and means to each learner while the goal and criterion stay common is expected to raise engagement and, where tailoring rests on a diagnosis of responses, aligned achievement, though no claim in the wiki tests personalization as a whole against uniform instruction and tailoring to learning styles is contradicted.
pages.title: Personalization

pages.description: For a beginning reader who cannot yet turn print into sound, explicit teaching of letter–sound correspondences in a planned sequence, applied at once to reading and spelling words, is expected to produce more accurate decoding and word reading than unsystematic or no phonics; a meta-analysis tests this for kindergarten to grade 6, with smaller gains for older struggling readers and for comprehension, and a contested advantage over whole-language teaching.
pages.title: Phonics

pages.description: For school-age learners whose on-task behavior drops during long seated stretches, a brief bout of movement between segments, followed by a named task, is expected to raise on-task behavior in the next segment but not test-measured attention or achievement; two classroom reviews and one school study test this for children, with the largest gain for the least on-task, and nothing in the wiki tests it for adults.
pages.title: Physical Activity

pages.description: For a learner who stalls, rushes or freezes at a predictable hard moment in a task, a few short, credible self-talk cues tied to a next action, modeled and rehearsed, are expected to improve performance and persistence; claims test self-talk only on sport and motor tasks, not on academic learning on its own.
pages.title: Positive Self-talk

pages.description: For a reader about to meet an expository text whose central ideas they do not yet know, attempting a few aligned questions before reading and checking the attempts against the text afterwards is expected to improve later memory of the questioned content over reading alone, possibly at some cost to unquestioned content; one laboratory claim tests this with undergraduates, and no claim tests its classroom, comprehension or purpose-setting forms.
pages.title: Pre-reading Questioning

pages.description: When learners are about to study material they do not yet know, asking them to attempt questions on it first, even though most attempts will be wrong, and then letting the study, lesson or feedback supply the answers, is expected to improve later memory of the questioned content over studying for the same time without the questions; laboratory and classroom studies recorded in the wiki test this, with the gain bounded to the questioned content, dependent on the answer arriving (immediately, for arbitrary paired items) and offset in one online course by learners who stopped.
pages.title: Pretesting (Prequestions Before Study)

pages.description: For learners new to a system or topic whose main lesson will use many unfamiliar parts or terms, a short primer giving the name, location and behaviour of each key component before that lesson is expected to improve transfer from it over the same lesson without a primer; claims in the wiki test this (Mayer's 5 of 5 experiments, median d = 0.85, and one VR experiment), bounded by prior knowledge, the complexity and pacing of the main lesson, and short lab tests.
pages.title: Pre-training Principle

pages.description: For learners who must apply knowledge to ill-structured problems, organizing work around problems has a small, highly variable and possibly inflated average effect; what is better supported is guidance for novices on the target content, with a problem-first phase as a narrower option followed by instruction.
pages.title: Problem-based Learning

pages.description: For a novice on a procedure, a visible model, supported attempts with feedback, support withdrawn on unaided success, then mixed practice spread over sessions with the steps tied to their reasons are expected to yield accurate, fluent, retained and flexible unaided performance; no claim tests the arc as a whole, only single links in it.
pages.title: Procedural Learning

pages.description: Teaching writing as a staged process (plan, draft, respond, revise, edit) with feedback on drafts gives developing writers a modest gain in writing quality over product-focused teaching, tested by one meta-analysis in grades 1–12 that found no gain for struggling writers, who gain more from explicit strategy instruction.
pages.title: Process-based Writing

pages.description: When the goal is conceptual understanding and transfer of a new concept, having learners first attempt problems that the concept solves, before they are taught it, and then teaching it by building on their attempts, is expected to improve conceptual knowledge and transfer over teaching first, with no pooled gain on procedural skill.
pages.title: Productive Failure

pages.description: For adult learners, deliberate early relationship work by the instructor (learning about each learner, greeting by name, stated working terms, a brief one-to-one, low-exposure participation before public, non-punitive responses to conflict) is expected to raise willingness to participate, raise needs and engage opposing arguments, but no claim in the wiki tests this for adults: the evidence is correlational syntheses and randomised tests of single moves in middle schools.
pages.title: Build productive instructor-learner relationships so adults feel connected and take an active role in learning

pages.description: For learners using a simulation, practice tool or AI assistant, building the productive use into the tool (obvious productive actions, controls that invite comparison, limits on shortcuts such as answer-giving) is expected to yield more of the intended activity and better unaided performance than the same tool governed by written directions; no claim in the wiki compares the two directly, and one randomised trial shows a hints-only limit preventing harm without producing a gain.
pages.title: Design tools so productive usage is guaranteed by affordances and constraints rather than instructions

pages.description: For a student writer who will revise a draft, a response that names specific strengths of the text alongside a few prioritised critical comments is expected to keep the writer acting on the critique and to improve the revision, more than critique alone or generic or ability praise; no claim in the wiki tests this, and the nearest evidence (feedback meta-analyses, praise experiments with children, AI feedback audits) bounds it.
pages.title: Provide positive comments alongside constructive criticism when responding to student writing

pages.description: For a learner doing attention-heavy work (reading, writing, problem solving, test preparation), a protected block with competing talk, notifications and avoidable interruptions removed is expected to lengthen on-task work and improve task performance compared with the same task amid ordinary distraction; no claim in the wiki tests this, and the nearest evidence is observational work on classroom conditions and surveys of study space and digital distraction.
pages.title: Quiet Learning Spaces

pages.description: When a picture, diagram or animation is explained by narration, adding on-screen text that repeats the narration word for word is expected to lower transfer for novices, most in system-paced lessons; when no picture competes for the eyes, the same words spoken and written do no harm and help second-language, less fluent and low-prior-knowledge readers, and text that helps novices becomes redundant as expertise grows. Claims test this: Mayer's experiments, a meta-analysis of verbal redundancy, a 63-study review and a meta-meta-analysis, with boundary conditions for pictures, pacing, reader fluency, prior knowledge, outcome and age.
pages.title: Redundancy Principle

pages.description: For a learner who has just performed a task or acted in a practice setting, structured prompts to examine that performance against a stated criterion and commit to a change are expected to improve later performance more than unguided reflection, qualified by the learner's ability to judge their own work, access to feedback, and whether the planned change is acted on.
pages.title: Reflection

pages.description: For learners whose ideas on a concept or principle may diverge from the plan, a teacher who makes their thinking visible, reads it against a prepared model of likely ideas and chooses the next move from it is expected to improve conceptual understanding and near transfer over the same plan delivered unchanged; no claim in the wiki tests this directly.
pages.title: Responsive Teaching

pages.description: For learners who have studied material, recalling it from memory rather than restudying tends to raise delayed retention when initial retrieval mostly succeeds or is corrected by feedback; restudy can lead at a few minutes, transfer gains are smaller and conditional, and high element-interactivity material is contested.
pages.title: Retrieval Practice

pages.description: For a learner who presents ideas the same way to every reader, teaching rhetorical moves as choices made for a stated audience, purpose and situation, with explicit criteria for evidence and for answering the other side, practice across contrasting situations, process goals first and learners saying why a move works, is expected to produce better arguments and better-fitted texts or talk than teaching fixed forms or style rules; no claim here tests that comparison, though argument practice, writing strategy instruction, real audiences and peer feedback are each tested.
pages.title: Rhetorical Skill Development

pages.description: Temporary support given while a learner attempts a task they cannot yet complete alone may improve later cognitive outcomes compared with unsupported attempts, qualified by the learner's task-specific starting response, the kind of support, the setting and whether the outcome is measured without the support.
pages.title: Scaffolding

pages.description: Contingent support that is withdrawn as the learner shows unaided success may improve later independent performance on a task the learner cannot yet do alone, qualified by the task-specific starting response, how support ends, the setting and the outcome horizon.
pages.title: Scaffolding and Fading

pages.description: When a lesson presents complex material as a continuous, transient stream (a narrated animation, a video, a live demonstration) to learners for whom its steps are new, presenting it in meaningful segments with a pause or a continue control between them is expected to improve retention and transfer over one continuous presentation, at the cost of more learning time; meta-analyses test this, and it holds when the system sets the pauses, matters more for complex than for simple material, and its relation to prior knowledge is mixed.
pages.title: Segmenting Principle

pages.description: For learners who expect an evaluation to confirm a negative judgement of their group or of them, a 10–15 minute private essay on a personally important value, given to the whole class before the threat, is expected to protect later grades compared with writing about an unimportant value; one claim tests this, with two positive small field experiments and a null large replication, so effects are small and unpredictable.
pages.title: Self Affirmation

pages.description: Handing a learner decisions about goals, resources, pace, strategy and evaluation is expected to sustain engagement and build independence without costing learning only when the learner knows enough about the content to choose well, has been taught to plan, monitor and evaluate in the subject, and is given control gradually with checked checkpoints; no claim in the wiki compares learner-directed with teacher-directed study directly.
pages.title: Self-Directed Learning

pages.description: For a learner with a readable criterion and a next move for each result, taught, test-based checks of their own work at set points during a task are expected to improve performance on it, but no claim here isolates self-monitoring against its absence on a learning outcome.
pages.title: Self-monitoring

pages.description: When learners are explicitly taught and prompted to plan, monitor against stated criteria and act on what they notice, their regulation activity and task performance may improve, qualified by monitoring accuracy, prior knowledge, whether support is used, and which outcome is measured.
pages.title: Self-Regulated Learning

pages.description: For a novice on a target whose parts depend on each other, meeting the parts in an order that puts what a step rests on before it and moves from what the learner can process toward full complexity, revised from the learner's responses, is expected to improve performance on tasks that draw on the whole; no claim tests that general rule, and tests of particular orders (example or problem first, parts or whole first, blocked or mixed) favour different orders for different learners and goals.
pages.title: Sequencing

pages.description: When learners study material whose essential elements and organisation they cannot yet pick out for themselves, adding cues that highlight those elements and how they connect (headings, an outline, highlighting, arrows, colour links between words and picture, spoken emphasis) is expected to improve learning over the same material without cues, by a small-to-medium amount in the meta-analyses the wiki records; the claims test this directly and report it weakening or reversing for learners who already know the material, and helping only for what is cued.
pages.title: Signaling Principle

pages.description: For a learner preparing for a risky, costly, rare or invisible performance, repeated runs in a simulation that keeps the task's decisions and cues, guided during exploration and followed by feedback or a debrief, are expected to improve performance on the represented task more than no simulated practice, with more immersion adding nothing by itself; claims test simulation against no intervention, passive and active instruction (no advantage over active methods) and guided against free VR exploration, but not the debrief, dose or fidelity.
pages.title: Simulations & Immersive Virtual Environments

pages.description: For learners who can already do the component skills, a short time-boxed cycle around one scoped deliverable, with criteria set before work starts, a mid-cycle review and revision, and an unhurried structured debrief, is expected to build whole-task skill better than open-ended projects or isolated exercises; no claim in the wiki tests sprints, and the evidence is on goals, feedback, coaching, reflection and time pressure in other settings.
pages.title: Skills Sprint

pages.description: For learners who can contribute to a multi-week group task, making the group's success depend on every member's individually assessed learning (a shared goal, team recognition built from individual results, and distinct roles or resources) is expected to make members help and hold one another to account and so raise individual achievement; claims test the reward-plus-accountability component in school studies, while one online experiment found role or reward structures changed interaction and attitudes but not achievement.
pages.title: Social Interdependence

pages.description: For learners in an online or blended group course whose part in discussion is thin or guarded, designed chances to be seen and heard as a person (course-tied introductions, a visible instructor, small stable groups, structured replies, some live contact) are expected to raise open participation and persistence, but the wiki holds only survey associations and correlational syntheses, and no claim tests that design on learning.
pages.title: Social Presence

pages.description: A conditional model relating learner state, activity and subsequent observation; the linked pattern specifies a reusable design policy.
pages.title: Spaced Learning

pages.description: A standardized test score is expected to support a selection or placement decision equally well across groups only where its items do not depend on group background, it predicts the later outcome equally accurately for each group, and the testing conditions do not depress one group's scores; no claim tests this relationship, and the claims bearing on it are second-hand testimony, narrative reviews, psychometric studies of item-bias methods and a values-affirmation intervention that did not replicate.
pages.title: Standardized Test Fairness and Bias

pages.description: For a learner described mainly by gaps, collecting evidence of what they can already do, naming it as specific performances and building tasks, roles and support from it, with barriers still addressed, is expected to raise teacher expectations, make competence visible and support self-efficacy and persistence; no claim here compares it with deficit-organized instruction, and praise of the person or brief belief exercises limit it.
pages.title: Strengths-based Approach

pages.description: An end-of-unit or end-of-course judgment is expected to report a capability fairly, and steer study towards it, when it samples the capability at the outcome's level with several tasks, uses criteria and a cut set in advance, follows low-stakes practice of the same thinking, and adds no demand such as speed or anxiety that the capability lacks; no claim here tests summative assessment as a design.
pages.title: Summative Assessment

pages.description: For young children building a first language, frequent responsive exchanges in which an adult answers and expands the child's own turns are expected to grow the child's expressive language more than language the child only hears; one routine, dialogic shared reading, is tested against ordinary reading, and the general relationship rests on associational evidence.
pages.title: Support Early Language Development

pages.description: For a student whose work on a unit shows the target already done, replacing the practice they do not need with acceleration or harder enrichment, chosen from that response rather than the label, is expected to sustain progress and engagement; no claim tests this, so the page gives a labelled default design.
pages.title: Supporting Gifted and Talented Students

pages.description: For a student with an intellectual disability who is not yet doing an age-appropriate academic or daily-life task, teaching it in small steps with more practice, specific feedback on what the student did, functional everyday contexts and full participation in the class is expected to raise performance and participation more than lowered expectations or separate, younger-age materials, though no claim in the wiki tests this combination; neighbouring claims test mastery pacing, mnemonics, self-determination instruction, student-led IEPs and praise.
pages.title: Supporting Students with Intellectual Disabilities

pages.description: For a team introducing an innovation that others must adopt, mapping the system it enters, planning the other changes it needs as one coordinated bundle and working on whichever part blocks now is expected to produce more lasting use than introducing the innovation alone; no claim in the wiki tests this, and the evidence is mostly the change literature's own argument.
pages.title: Guide change efforts with systemic understanding, focusing interventions on one framework component at a time as needed

pages.description: For learners meeting content they must understand, especially through a second language, moving lesson time from teacher talk to learners' own purposeful talk and short writing about the content, in a class where mistakes are safe, is expected to deepen understanding and willingness to speak; no claim tests this whole relationship, writing-to-learn and discussion-versus-lecture claims test its halves, and more talk alone does not raise comprehension.
pages.title: Treat talking and writing as means to learning through dialogue-based, student-centered instruction

pages.description: For an L2 learner who produces a form but distributes it unlike proficient users because the L1 divides the meaning differently, explaining the meaning that motivates the form's uses (its core sense, with diagrams) and then practising choices across contexts is expected to yield more appropriate use than structural or phrase-only teaching; no claim in the wiki tests this comparison.
pages.title: Teach the conceptual underpinnings of L2 forms rather than only their structural aspects or formulaic units

pages.description: For learners working toward understanding they can use, a teacher who states the goal, organizes a task learners act on, questions and helps contingently while they work, and has them explain and transfer what they understood is expected to yield more engagement and usable understanding than presenting the content, provided novices still get explicit guidance; no claim in the wiki tests the teacher's role directly, only neighbouring comparisons (active learning against lecture, teacher-led against student-led inquiry).
pages.title: Educators should act as mediators and facilitators of learning rather than content disseminators

pages.description: For a teacher who needs families' cooperation, relationship-first contact and regular two-way communication about learning, begun before any problem, are expected to build more teacher-parent trust and fewer escalations than relying on rules notices and remote sanctions; no claim tests that comparison, though partnership-programme trials and a home-visit study test parts of it.
pages.title: Strengthen ties between teachers and parents rather than pressing for remote sanctions behind teaching

pages.description: When a tool could do part of a task the learner must learn to do unaided, using it so the learner still does that part (attempt first; hints, questions and feedback rather than solutions; simulation or VR beside hands-on practice, not instead of it) is expected to give better performance once the tool is removed than letting it take the part over; single studies of generative AI with adults test this, three experiments limit it, and no claim tests complement against replacement for simulation or VR.
pages.title: Technology should augment, not supplant, learning processes in student-centered environments

pages.description: For learners who need practice writing for a live audience or a lower-threshold way to ask and respond, a focused text chat on a closed task, with content prepared beforehand and someone keeping the pace legible, is expected to produce negotiation of meaning, self-correction and wider participation, but no claim in the wiki tests chat against the same task without it on a learning outcome.
pages.title: Text Chats

pages.description: For a learner whose barrier to a text is decoding, vision or fatigue rather than its language, and when the goal is its meaning rather than reading the words, hearing the text read aloud while following the print with control of pace is expected to raise comprehension over print alone; no claim in the wiki tests text-to-speech itself.
pages.title: Text-to-Speech

pages.description: Showing the same structure in several surface forms, prompting learners to compare them and name what they share, and then having them retrieve and apply it on changed items is expected to raise near transfer to new cases once the original learning is secure; no claim tests varied against single-context instruction directly, and far transfer stayed at floor where it was measured.
pages.title: Transfer of Learning

pages.description: For a learner who can make attempts at a new concept or principle, exploration guided by clues, questions on the learner's own ideas and critique of everyone's work, with the principle then named from that work, is expected to deepen understanding more than being told first or exploring unguided, though no claim tests indirect against direct guidance.
pages.title: Understanding must be cultivated through exploration, not described or told

pages.description: For a class whose learners vary in access, language, prior knowledge and motivation, planning several routes into content, engagement and expression while the goal and criteria stay fixed is expected to let more learners reach the goal than a single-route design; no claim here tests UDL as a framework, only its parts.
pages.title: Universal Design For Learning

pages.description: In kindergarten to grade 3, briefly screening every child for early reading risk at set points in the year and following each flag within weeks with a diagnostic look and added instruction is expected to find children who need help sooner than referral; the wiki holds no test of screening itself, and its evidence (mostly one Massachusetts research programme) shows screeners flag later strugglers better than they clear the rest, disagree with each other, and flag children from low-income families, English learners and Black and Hispanic children more often, gaps that reflect circumstances, treatment and possibly the measure, not the children.
pages.title: Universal Early Literacy Screening

pages.description: For learners who reach instruction through a digital interface, revising that interface against what representative users actually do on the real learning tasks (finding, reading, submitting, interpreting) is expected to remove avoidable effort and failed attempts that compete with the content, though no claim in the wiki compares a user-tested interface with an untested one on a learning outcome.
pages.title: User-Centered Design for Learning

pages.description: A classroom assessment score is expected to support a decision about a learner only as far as the tasks sample the intended capability without demands unrelated to it, the score is consistent across items, occasions and raters, and no group is disadvantaged by content or administration; no claim here tests that relationship in classrooms, and the claims that bear on it come mostly from large-scale testing and simulations.
pages.title: Validity, Reliability, and Bias in Classroom Assessment

pages.description: For a learner building a real-time performance skill who cannot yet say accurately what they did at the moments that mattered, reviewing a recording against one stated focus, explaining paused moments, debriefing with someone who asks before telling and carrying one change into a recorded next attempt is expected to improve what they notice and their next performance, though no claim tests reviewing one's own recording against an alternative; the evidence is coaching reports, one study of teacher candidates analysing others' video, and findings carried from self-explanation and contingent support.
pages.title: Video Replay Analysis

pages.description: When critical feedback crosses a racial or ethnic difference, or reaches a learner from a group stereotyped in the domain, specific task-level critique stated together with the high standard it is held to and an explicit assurance that the learner can reach it is expected to be trusted and acted on more than the same critique without that framing; no claim in the wiki tests this, and neighbouring brief identity-targeted interventions are fragile.
pages.title: Wise Feedback Across Racial and Ethnic Difference

pages.description: An example-first relationship qualified by task knowledge, representation, configuration and assessment horizon.
pages.title: Worked Examples

pages.description: The article argues motivational studies lack systematicity and linkage between theory and practice, and proposes pairing a generic instructional design process with a motivational model: \"The ADDIE process is geared t...
pages.title: Use a systematic instructional design process (ADDIE) with a motivational model to diagnose and address motivational problems

pages.description: Glaser's design orientation sets a task sequence: specify the terminal performance standard, determine student entry characteristics and prerequisites, construct procedures and materials to move the learner from one s...
pages.title: Analyze terminal behavior and objectives before manipulating teaching methods in instructional design

pages.description: A post-release design process that treats a shipped course as a hypothesis under test — instrumenting materials so that use and outcome data are collected together, running short build–measure–learn cycles, and using RISE analysis to decide which resource to revise next.
pages.title: Continuous Improvement of Learning Materials

pages.description: The Data Wise Improvement Process is an eight-step, team-based protocol for using student assessment data to drive instructional improvement in schools.
pages.title: Data Wise Improvement Process

pages.description: A design process run as research. An intervention is designed and revised over repeated cycles in a real learning setting, in collaboration with practitioners, so that each cycle both improves the design and builds or tests theory about learning.
pages.title: Design-Based Research

pages.description: A course-grain design process — empathize, define, ideate, prototype, test — in which a learning experience is built from investigated learner need rather than from a content outline, and revised against evidence from learners before it is finalized.
pages.title: Design Thinking

pages.description: The design process as it actually runs in higher education — an instructor designing their own course, part-time, alongside teaching it, with a teaching centre consulting rather than approving, and revision happening between offerings rather than within a project.
pages.title: Faculty Course Design

pages.description: Composing a grade requires teachers to make several separable, often-unexamined decisions — how to weight components, whether to fold in social skills or effort, and whether to grade absolutely or relatively — each with real tradeoffs that a single "best" answer doesn't resolve.
pages.title: Grading Policy Decisions

pages.description: A co-design facilitation structure that deliberately makes space for educators' affective and relational experience — through shared contemplative practice, ritualized check-ins, and reflective field-note protocols — treating emotion as a design resource rather than a distraction.
pages.title: Humanizing Co-Design with Educators

pages.description: This development pattern adapts an intervention-development framework to build a descriptive clinical instrument through repeated cycles of drafting, expert consultation, piloting, feasibility testing, and refinement,...
pages.title: Iterative, stakeholder-informed instrument development cycle

pages.description: A user-centred course design process that treats usability as a pedagogical property rather than presentation polish — investigating learners, prototyping the experience, and testing it with real users, on the argument that effort spent operating the material is effort not spent learning.
pages.title: Learner Experience Design (LXD)

pages.description: The guide's central design principle is devolving compliance assurance to the local level: districts perform a compliance self-review that the state agency later validates, with state technical and management assistan...
pages.title: Increase local responsibility for program compliance through self-review before state validation

pages.description: The report stresses that the standard application of the body of work method involves two distinct phases: range-finding, where work samples cover the entire range sparsely, and pin-pointing, which uses only samples n...
pages.title: Include both range-finding and pin-pointing phases when applying the body of work method

pages.description: An iterative, agile course design process that replaces a single analyse-build-evaluate pass with short rounds of design, prototype and review, starting from a collaborative Savvy Start and converging on a design by repeated approximation rather than by up-front specification.
pages.title: Successive Approximation Model (SAM)

pages.description: The objective-first design process — ADDIE and the Dick & Carey systems approach — in which instructional goals are analysed into subordinate skills, assessments are written from the objectives, instruction is built to serve them, and formative evaluation feeds revision before the design is released.
pages.title: Systematic Instructional Design

pages.description: The task-centred design process that produces a 4C/ID blueprint — specify the professional tasks first, group them into task classes of equal complexity ordered simple to complex, then derive the supporting theory and part-task practice from the tasks rather than the other way round.
pages.title: Ten Steps to Complex Learning

pages.description: Wiggins and McTighe's backward design process plans a course or unit in three stages — identify desired results, determine acceptable evidence, then plan learning experiences — so that activities and assessments are derived from the learning goals rather than chosen first and justified afterward.
pages.title: Understanding by Design

pages.description: The contract production process used by e-learning studios — macro design, storyboard, then alpha, beta and gold builds, each ending in a client review, with the final sign-off closing the design to further change.
pages.title: Vendor Production (Alpha–Beta–Gold)

pages.description: A 10-item, 5-point Likert self-report questionnaire developed by Markus H.
pages.title: 10-item self-report questionnaire for critical use of genAI

pages.description: A 100-term botanical vocabulary and information test developed by Grier for assessing first-year high-school pupils' plant-life knowledge carried from nature study and school gardens.
pages.title: 100-word range of information test in botany

pages.description: A competency framework developed by Zolo Yvan et al.
pages.title: 11-cluster competency framework for academic global surgery education

pages.description: A Krieglstein et al.
pages.title: 15-item theory-based cognitive load questionnaire

pages.description: A 16-item paper-and-pencil assessment for upper-secondary students that measures hypothesis formulation, experiment design, data representation, variable relationships, and error identification.
pages.title: 16-item paper-and-pencil test of inquiry skills

pages.description: A restricted dataset of 1,650 educator- and student-submitted STEM questions containing structurally meaningful diagrams for evaluating AI interpretation of topological reasoning, collected and curated by Sun et al.
pages.title: 1,650-question STEM diagram dataset collected via campus-wide submission campaign

pages.description: A research dataset created by Zhao et al.
pages.title: 168-essay three-draft-type corpus with standardized ChatGPT-4 revision prompt

pages.description: An 18-item, rater-administered observation instrument developed by Hijzen et al.
pages.title: 18-item engagement rating list for observing CL engagement

pages.description: A school-level reporting instrument developed by Anthony Bryk and colleagues that synthesizes student and teacher survey responses for comparison, self-analysis, and school-improvement planning.
pages.title: 1997 Improving Chicago's Schools Individual School Report

pages.description: A 20-item five-point Likert-type scale developed by Koparan et al.
pages.title: 20-item Attitude Towards Statistics (ATS) scale developed by the researchers

pages.description: A Chicago Public Schools survey administered to students, teachers, and principals in 2003 to collect information about school experiences, instruction, professional development, and working conditions.
pages.title: 2003 Improving Chicago's Schools survey

pages.description: A spring 2005 survey administered across Chicago Public Schools by the Consortium on Chicago School Research to collect reports from students, teachers, and principals about school experiences, instruction, professional development, and working conditions.
pages.title: 2005 Improving Chicago's Schools survey

pages.description: A CCSR-developed survey and school-reporting instrument used with Chicago Public Schools AVID students and teachers to measure program experiences and compare participating schools.
pages.title: 2007 CPS AVID student and teacher survey with individualized school reports

pages.description: A questionnaire developed by Czerniewicz et al.
pages.title: 2007 South African ICT access and use survey with 26 ICT-mediated activities categorised by Laurillard's Conversational Framework

pages.description: A NWEA release of national achievement and growth norms, percentiles, and norms tables for MAP Growth assessments across U.S.
pages.title: 2025 MAP Growth Achievement and Growth Norms

pages.description: An internationally collected survey dataset of 211 educators across nine countries and education levels, released by Matt Bower et al., documenting the generative-AI tools educators reported using across nine typology categories.
pages.title: 2026 GenAI Typology survey dataset of educator tool usage

pages.description: A smartphone-based intensive longitudinal dataset from 92 adult foreign-language learners, capturing momentary emotions, perceived proficiency, and contextual features across 21 days.
pages.title: 21-day EMA dataset of 6,918 language-learning episodes with momentary emotions, perceived proficiency and contextual features

pages.description: A statewide California initiative administered by UC Berkeley's State Center in partnership with UCLA and the California Subject Matter Project that provides free professional learning, communities of practice, and coaching for PreK–12 educational leaders.
pages.title: 21st Century California School Leadership Academy (21CSLA)

pages.description: A U.S.
pages.title: 21st Century Community Learning Centers (21st CCLC) program

pages.description: Researcher-designed achievement-test and questionnaire instruments developed by Oso Senny Oluwatumbi for evaluating students' achievement and ICT-related knowledge and skills in e-classroom and conventional classroom conditions.
pages.title: 21st Century E-Classroom Achievement Test (ECAT) and E-classroom questionnaire (ECQ)

pages.description: A five-point Likert-scale instrument developed by Fan Bu et al.
pages.title: 22-item self-report instrument measuring contextual support, trust calibration, collaborative regulation, and perceived transfer gains

pages.description: A 23-item, seven-domain Likert survey instrument adapted and translated by Tuan Thanh Nguyen to measure Vietnamese EFL learners’ acceptance and intended use of mobile-assisted language learning.
pages.title: 23-item Meta-UTAUT survey instrument for MALL usage in EFL

pages.description: A 24-item orally administered questionnaire developed by Gunderson et al.
pages.title: 24-item motivational frameworks questionnaire (intelligence and sociomoral domains)

pages.description: A 25-item researcher-developed chemistry achievement test measuring Senior Secondary 2 students' understanding of stoichiometry and the mole concept, used as a pre-test and post-test in the study.
pages.title: 25-item Chemistry Achievement Test (CAT) on stoichiometry and mole concept

pages.description: A 25-item multiple-choice test developed by Alneyadi et al.
pages.title: 25-item electronic magnetism cognitive achievement test
